title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
description: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.The clip used Larsson'
body: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun". In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people.""The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future". "It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life. White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda". Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

schema.headline: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video

title: Spotted wildcat from Bolivian forest revealed as new species
description: Only one confirmed member of the species is known - a cat living in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.It was this 10
body: Only one confirmed member of the species is known - a cat living in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery. Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens."There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia.

schema.headline: Spotted wildcat from Bolivian forest revealed as new species

title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
description: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military
body: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region"."The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added.Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron.This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external.Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian

schema.headline: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial

title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
description: Image source, Metropolitan PoliceImage caption, Ukrainian Illia Bilyk, 21, pleaded guilty to carrying out a string of vandalism attacks in LondonByDan
body: Image source, Metropolitan PoliceImage caption, Ukrainian Illia Bilyk, 21, pleaded guilty to carrying out a string of vandalism attacks in LondonByDaniel De SimoneInvestigations correspondent and Tom BealAt Thames Magistrates' CourtA Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage.Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council.The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram.Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards.In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising. Image source, Leyton Jamia MasjidImage caption, Bilyk (bottom right corner) spraying graffiti on Leyton Jamia Masjid in January 2025Lavrynovych, who personally started the fires targeting Sir Keir's property, also admitted spraying Islamophobic graffiti on an Islamic building in south London.He was recruited on Telegram and offered money by an anonymous handler, known by the initials EL, for the graffiti and the arson attacks.EL was a Russian operative who organised a widespread sabotage and provocation campaign remotely through social media and Telegram.EL was centrally involved in running a fake far-right group called Direct Action UK, which was created by Russian operatives to provoke acts of vandalism on British streets, including the graffiti attacks on mosques.After Bilyk sprayed his abusive graffiti in east London in January 2025, images of the attacks were shared in a Direct Action Telegram group.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A Russia-linked group tied to the arson attack against the former UK prime minister shared images of graffiti sprayed by Ukrainian man Illia BilykHours after two of his attacks, EL posted in a jobs group for Ukrainian people offering money for pictures of buildings in the area.The BBC investigation named a Russian diplomat, Evgeny Lyukshin, who was part of the Direct Action UK chat group. Lyukshin was trained in "information warfare" by senior Russian spies and his details matched those of EL. He did not respond to the BBC.Bilyk will be sentenced on 19 October at Stratford Magistrates' Court.Chief Superintendent Rhona Hunt, from the Met Police, said: "We recognise that these incidents caused significant distress within Muslim communities across east London last year and that they continue to cause concern."Anti-Muslim hate crime and Islamophobia have absolutely no place in London. We are committed to tackling hate crime while supporting and reassuring our communities."

schema.headline: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack

title: Man City 5-0 Norwich: Floyd Samba debut overshadows JJ Gabriel saga
description: Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from anoth
body: Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester.Website articles, social media posts and column inches have been filled this week with the news that highly rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United.But that particular saga will be overshadowed in Friday's football cuttings by 17-year-old Samba's stunning bow on the professional stage, scoring twice in Manchester City's 5-0 Carabao Cup third-round thrashing of Norwich City.Samba was prolific in City's under-18 side last season and those impressive performances led to him being promoted to the first-team set-up by new manager Enzo Maresca this summer.The show of faith is already being repaid."I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team," Samba told BBC Radio 5 Live. "To get a debut like that is mind-blowing."I couldn't believe it myself - but that is just the beginning, I have got a big career ahead of me. It was a great debut."I spoke to all of them [first-team players], they have all been brilliant with me - before the game, giving me advice like 'play your game, be you' - those words have given me confidence and helped me score those two goals today."The youngster joined City's academy at under-nine level and he really started to make a name for himself last term.Samba scored 24 goals and provided 10 assists in an eye-catching first full season with the under-18s, including curling home a stunning free-kick to help City win the FA Youth Cup final against rivals Manchester United in May.On his debut, Samba played the entire 90 minutes and fully grasped his opportunity.With City struggling for openings, Samba broke the deadlock by flicking home a header - he celebrated by blowing a kiss in the direction of family and friends in the stands, before curling in a delightful second later in the game.Samba was afforded a generous ovation towards the end of the game when being deservedly named man of the match."[I'm] satisfied not just for the goals but for the performance too," said manager Maresca."I asked him in the last three, four days - when I decided to play him as nine - he said he never played there. He is not a nine for sure, but he was good."He is young, full of energy, strong, can finish, can set [players up]. He made some good decisions in the first half. I am happy but they are young and we have to go slowly, slowly."Hopefully we can give him more chances."The Samba surname will be familiar to those of a certain age who have followed the Premier League.Floyd is the son of former Blackburn and QPR defender Christopher, who played 171 top-flight matches for those two sides, as well as a further 12 in the Championship with Aston Villa.The City forward is the younger of two brothers at the club, with Tyrone also involved in the youth team, and will now be aiming to play more first-team minutes after an exciting debut.As a fleet-footed forward, Floyd could not be more of a different player to his dad Christopher, who was a no-nonsense towering centre-back."Coming from under-21s to first-team training, that is a big jump," added Samba. "The sessions are more tiring, you have to run more - they demand more of you and you have to cope with it."Former Norwich striker Chris Sutton added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Absolutely brilliant moment for Floyd. His dad was in the stadium and will be extremely proud. It's the journey, he has been nurtured at Man City, got his moment and what a night for him."He has given Enzo Maresca a bit of food for thought moving forward. Of course, he is not going to play ahead of Erling Haaland but it is a great evening for him and good for his development."Maresca can think he can trust him a little bit more."

schema.headline: Man City 5-0 Norwich: Floyd Samba debut overshadows JJ Gabriel saga

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton and Liam Dawson impress as hosts secure T20 series win in Cardiff
description: Second Vitality T20, CardiffSri Lanka 145-9 (20 overs): Nissanka 37 (21); Dawson 3-32England 146-4 (12.1 overs): Banton 52* (24); Rathnayake 1-25Engla
body: Second Vitality T20, CardiffSri Lanka 145-9 (20 overs): Nissanka 37 (21); Dawson 3-32England 146-4 (12.1 overs): Banton 52* (24); Rathnayake 1-25England won by six wickets; lead series 2-0ScorecardEngland's impressive T20 form continued as they thrashed Sri Lanka by six wickets in Cardiff to seal the series with a match to spare. Tom Banton's unbeaten 52 ensured England made light work of chasing a below-par 146, reaching the target in just 12.1 overs. Jos Buttler and Aneurin Donald raced to an opening stand of 51 in 4.3 overs before they both fell in the space of four balls for 30 and 21 respectively, but England's middle order followed suit in their aggression.Captain Harry Brook needed to score 49 to break Tilak Varma's record of 336 T20 international runs without being dismissed, and he looked on course, whacking three sixes in his 23 off just eight balls, before he was brilliantly caught by a diving Eshan Malinga.Banton then took on the charge, clubbing four sixes in his 24-ball knock as England remain unbeaten in the shortest format this summer.Brendon McCullum's side have now won 22 of their past 25 completed T20s since the start of last summer - a win percentage of 88%, with India (73%) the next best among full-member nations.England's fluency juxtaposed Sri Lanka's innings as the tourist batters struggled again, limping to 145-9 after being bowled out for just 135 in the opener on Tuesday.There will be added frustration from this innings, though, as their openers started so brightly by reaching 55-0 from the first five overs. But Liam Dawson took two wickets in the final over of the powerplay to halt their momentum and the middle order failed to recover, losing 9-90 thereafter and adding just 12 from a dire final four overs. Dawson finished with 3-32 and Jamie Overton 2-23, while Sonny Baker impressed again with his pace and control in a miserly spell of 1-15, including a wicket maiden in the 19th over.The series concludes at Old Trafford on Saturday and is followed by three one-day internationals.Though it is proving to be a mismatched series so far, England are building a well-balanced line-up under Brook's leadership and have barely broken sweat in notching a 2-0 lead.Sri Lanka's explosive start, led by Pathum Nissanka, who top-scored with 37, was the only time England have been on the back foot, but it was the ever-reliable Dawson who dragged it back, having become a mainstay in Brook's T20 line-up. The two soft dismissals highlighted Sri Lanka's woes - Lahiru Udara was caught at mid-on and Kamil Mishara chipped one straight back to the slow left-arm spinner. What followed was a series of soft dismissals, most caught trying to find the boundary, as Overton and Baker hammered away at a good length before Archer, who had started expensively, claimed two wickets at the death to revive his own figures.Sri Lanka managed just two sixes in their innings compared to England's 10, with it being only the seventh time their top five have all hit at least one in T20 internationals.Newcomer Donald started the carnage, ramping Dushmantha Chameera's first ball over the ropes, before Buttler joined the party and Brook then launched three of his own into the stands.England's intent was clear from the fact Donald's strike-rate of 161.54 was the lowest of the top five. Spinner Wanindu Hasaranga took most of the damage as he conceded 42 off just three overs, with a couple disappearing out of the ground.Banton, one of few batters to miss out in England's 254-4 on Tuesday, made the most of his opportunity to produce a fine finish by sweeping and striking firmly down the ground.England have set themselves up nicely to finish unbeaten in T20s this summer after thrashing India 4-0 earlier in the year.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton and Liam Dawson impress as hosts secure T20 series win in Cardiff

title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
description: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's dea
body: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday.For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict.On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities.The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes.The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US.They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice.The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities.Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes.They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles.The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM.In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects".The fact-finding mission's report also covers the Iranian authorities' violent repression of the mass protests that took place across Iran in December 2025 and January 2026.The experts said it was an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests.They cited witnesses, health workers and victims' families as saying that security personnel positioned themselves on rooftops and other elevated positions, firing their assault rifles into crowds.Protesters also sustained severe wounds to the head, chest and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness.As the crackdown escalated, security forces attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded demonstrators and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care, according to the experts.They also found that the tens of thousands of people detained during the protests faced torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal counsel.The experts warned that the government had since intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters, with at least 29 men executed following expedited trials on charges connected to the unrest.The fact-finding mission's report noted that it was not possible to independently verify the death toll from the crackdown, but said there were strong grounds to believe that it was significantly higher than the official figure of 3,000, the majority of whom the government identified as members of the security forces or bystanders.The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) has said it has confirmed the killing of more than 7,000 people, almost all of them protesters.The fact-finding mission's experts concluded that Iranian authorities had committed "many gross human rights violations" during the crackdown, and that these amounted to "the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts, committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against a civilian population".Iranian authorities accused the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest and blamed the deaths on what they described as "terrorists" and "rioters".

schema.headline: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes

title: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
description: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.This weekend more than 600 o
body: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.This weekend more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers are battling it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton."We've never had any media wanting to attend before," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.And though influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern."Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told the BBC he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue."Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said."I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language."Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting."It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".And Ginn said: "If elite means having some expertise in the sport over 20 odd years, I'm proud of that."Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games."Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.So what about the crocodiles?They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't referenced in the media release about the technical assessment. That report itself has not yet been made public.The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times."The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says."Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped tens of millions of dollars into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy."The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.And those who argue the tabloid-friendly crocodile debate is overblown, say the biggest of the creatures live downstream. The less-dangerous freshwater crocodiles are more likely to be spotted in the rowing arena, they say.Also contested by government is the flood risk, though Rowing Queensland's O'Loughlin says that their schools event was due to be held on the Fitzroy in August 2024, but had to be moved after the course was washed away.Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

schema.headline: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern

title: 'Putney pusher' investigation ongoing after suspect's death, police say
description: The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview"."They searched his home, and the Met Police press te
body: The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview"."They searched his home, and the Met Police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting," they said. "For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence."He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation."They said the police were repeatedly asked to end their investigation and warned about the impact it was having on Brandram's mental health, adding: "Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead."Brandram was linked to the incident in April when a person contacted officers with information that opened new lines of inquiry, according to the Met. His arrest was deemed proportionate by officers in order to seize and search his devices as part of the investigation. The force emphasised that it had not named Brandram publicly when he was arrested or at any point before his death. While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.Ch Supt Dan Knowles said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram's family and friends at this deeply distressing time. "We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him."He said that following Brandram's release under investigation, "it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations"."This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing," he added.Knowles, who leads policing in south-west London, said that cases involving "complex evidential and forensic work" could take "a number of months to complete". The Independent Office of Police Conduct confirmed it had received the Met's referral, which is being assessed.Shortly after the Putney Bridge incident on 5 May 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head."It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me."The Met said at the time that about 15 minutes after the push, the jogger came back the other way across the bridge and ignored the victim when she tried to speak to him.Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident.The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: 'Putney pusher' investigation ongoing after suspect's death, police say

title: Bournemouth: From -17 to dream European start for Adam Smith and Cherries
description: 'From -17 to Europe', read a flag in the away end at at the Anoeta Stadium.As Bournemouth embarked on the first European campaign in the club's 127-ye
body: 'From -17 to Europe', read a flag in the away end at at the Anoeta Stadium.As Bournemouth embarked on the first European campaign in the club's 127-year history, it served as a reminder of just how far they have come.But a 2-1 victory at Real Sociedad in their Europa League opener shows they are not ready to stop there.It is now 11 years since the Cherries were first promoted to the Premier League, meaning there is now a generation of supporters who will view top-flight football as the norm.From that perspective then, qualifying and playing in Europe might simply appear the next logical step for a well-run and ambitious club."It's a brilliant win in our first European game. It's brilliant for the club and the 2,000 fans from Bournemouth," manager Marco Rose told TNT Sports.Yet for the vast majority of fans celebrating a famous victory on Thursday, the whole thing still seems surreal.Just 18 years ago, the club was on the brink. A 10-point deduction for entering administration resulted in their relegation to League Two.To even stay in the Football League for the 2008-09 season, they had to accept a 17-point deduction and agree not to appeal against the decision after it was ruled that, as they had been unable to agree a Company Voluntary Arrangement, they had not met their terms for exiting administration.Thoughts of a £100m-rated midfielder picking out a Brazil winger to head Bournemouth to victory in Europe was the stuff of fantasy as the Dorset club battled for survival.But that now is Bournemouth's reality with Alex Scott swaggering around San Sebastian, showing why there is such a clammer for his signature among top Premier League clubs, and Rayan providing another example of why the Cherries will demand every penny of a reported £130m release clause to let him go.Bournemouth have nothing to compare it to but this was a proper European away performance.Up against a Real Sociedad side led by a World Cup-winning forward in Mikel Oyarzabal and who beat Atletico Madrid to win the Copa del Rey last season, they were dominant for 45 minutes.They suffocated Sociedad with their relentlessness off the ball, winning the ball back high up the pitch time and again and showing the quality on the ball to create chances - even when the defence was set.But there is an edge to the Basque side and, poor as they had been, that they came out fighting after the break was no surprise.The adrenaline-fueled exuberance of Rose's side in the first half appeared to catch up with them in the second, but their desire to compete never wavered.Bournemouth are not known for their defensive resilience and, as Sociedad ramped up the pressure as the game wore on, thoughts might have turned to leads surrendered in each of their first four Premier League games.But the Cherries, aided by the sharp reflexes of Djordje Petrovic in goal, held on to secure a famous win."It was very intense and tough," Rose told TNT Sports."Brilliant first half in everything. The way we won balls and the possession high up. In the second half, we needed to suffer because we were not so sharp."Speaking on BBC Radio Solent, former Cherries full-back Charlie Daniels added: "It is a big occasion. A big moment for the club, and they should be applauded for it."Bournemouth's incredible rise can be traced back to the appointment of Eddie Howe in January 2009.The former boss guided the Cherries to safety, finishing nine points clear of the relegation zone despite that 17-point deduction.A mere six and a half years later, Howe - back for his second spell as manager - had taken a transformed Bournemouth to the Premier League.It was fitting then, that on this latest milestone night for the club, the team was led out by a man involved during Howe's first stint.Adam Smith joined Bournemouth on loan during the 2010-11 campaign, returned on a permanent deal in 2014 and has been at the club ever since, with approaching 400 league appearances to his name."Adam has been with the club for so long," Daniels said. "Dedicated himself to the club, and it's such a proud moment, not only for him, but for his family, his team-mates and old team-mates to see how he's grown - not only as a player but as a man as well."To lead out the Cherries on this historical night is fantastic."Smith also made history of his own, becoming, at 35 years and 141 days, the oldest English outfielder to make their debut in major European competition since Ipswich's Reginald Pickett in 1962.The club captain will appreciate more than most what a special night this was for Bournemouth.Things have been far from straightforward for the club, even in recent years, with relegation in 2020 and, since re-establishing themselves in the top-flight, the seemingly annual battle to replace players picked off by Europe's top clubs.Even qualifying for Europe was not enough to keep hold of manager Andoni Iraola, who returns to the Vitality Stadium with his new club Liverpool on Sunday.That pattern is unlikely to stop anytime soon but, while there is the prospect of more nights like this one, Bournemouth supporters won't be complaining.They've seen enough to know that these are the good times.

schema.headline: Bournemouth: From -17 to dream European start for Adam Smith and Cherries

title: England squad announcement: Big questions facing Thomas Tuchel
description: Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcom
body: Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut.Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach.He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo.But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia.Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back.Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party.It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton pair Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Jarrad Branthwaite are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list.Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup.That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players.Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury.Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men.But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame.Away from the height of those emotions in July, the Football Association is completing a review into England's World Cup campaign. The FA has been keen to stress that this assessment is a standard process, rather than an indication of wider concern or alarm about England's third-place finish.Indeed, key figures at the FA view the tournament in which England achieved their best finish since 1966 as a success, and the organisation has already backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.Tuchel and members of his backroom team gave their contributions to the review at St George's Park in late August. England players' opinions are also being gathered before a report is presented to senior bosses at the FA.The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament. After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.The content of the review won't be made public, but the next three weeks will give an indication of whether the camp is still as together as that night at the Azteca.

schema.headline: England squad announcement: Big questions facing Thomas Tuchel

title: Learner drivers use YouTube to cut costs but instructors warn of risks
description: Image caption, Megan is one of many people who used social media to help her learn to driveByLola MayorBBC NewsLearner drivers say they are turning to
body: Image caption, Megan is one of many people who used social media to help her learn to driveByLola MayorBBC NewsLearner drivers say they are turning to online tutorials to help with the cost of obtaining a driving licence.Driving lessons in the UK are now about £35 to £50, according to the RAC, with the average learner needing 45 hours of lessons and a further 22 hours of practice.Megan Kielthy, who passed her driving test in August, said social media videos "definitely" saved her money, but she also had seen AI-generated images and misinformation that she had warned could confuse learners.The Driving Instructors Association (DIA) said while digital education could be "excellent" it should go "hand in hand" with practical lessons, and that road safety was a matter of "life and death".Figure caption, BBC journalist Lola Mayor explains why some learner drivers are turning to social mediaMegan, 18, opted for a trainee instructor to save money but said learning to drive had still cost her more than £1,000.She earns £10 an hour babysitting, which she said had gone towards her £30 lessons alongside help from her parents."I don't think that I would have been able to do it without the financial support from my parents," she said."I found that having access to YouTube allowed me to cut costs."I would learn all the content with my instructor but then I was able to revisit content and then if there was something in a YouTube video that I didn't know, that I didn't fully understand, I was able to go back to my instructor and ask him."She added: "I had part of high school online because of Covid so I already knew how to use recorded content for learning so it felt very natural for me."Megan warned that not all of the content she had seen online had been helpful."I stumbled across an AI image of a roundabout showing which lane to be in for the exit and it just made no sense. I showed it to my driving instructor and he agreed it was ridiculous."If people solely relied on online content it could lead to people going on their test unprepared or misinformed of what they're going to experience on their test and driving after."Image caption, Betsi says young people are already facing financial barriers and learning to drive is a big commitmentThe total cost of learning to drive is about £2,460, according to the DIA, a rise of more than £570 since 2020, external.Learners also need to pay for a theory test at £23, a practical test at £65 and temporary driving insurance in personal cars which can cost £40-£50 a month.Betsi Seward, 18, is currently learning to drive alongside studying at college and working part-time."I am lucky I have a part-time job and can afford to fund it myself but if I didn't, it would be so difficult," she said."Over the last couple of months my whole TikTok and Instagram is just people learning to drive. It's like my algorithm knows, it's quite scary," she said."I find them helpful. I was practicing how to do an emergency stop and I was watching videos on how to do that and it really helped to see like where to put my foot on the clutch and stuff like that."But Betsi said not all the content she had seen was helpful. "When you post people making mistakes, that is what is going to get the attention and interaction," she said.She said there were also "random accounts of people using AI to generate mock tests like the routes... and it's obviously not real."But then if you're just learning to drive and you haven't had a few lessons, you wouldn't know that and it's quite scary actually, because if you take that information into the car with you and it's wrong, then it's quite dangerous actually and quite scary."Image source, SavannaImage caption, Savannah passed her test earlier this yearSavannah Jones, 20, from Cardiff, who works in childcare, passed her driving test in June.Her dad paid for her lessons, which totalled about £2,000."I'm very grateful. He was very chuffed when I passed first time," she said."I was watching a few YouTube videos. I saw a lot of TikToks. It was very much most of my algorithm was learning to drive, tips and tricks."I think it could help someone cut the cost but not for me personally. I would watch to understand it a bit more and apply that when learning."'It needs to be used responsibly'Image caption, John Reynolds says students are looking for more affordable ways to learn to driveJohn Reynolds has been a driving instructor for 13 years and started making his own social media videos last year.These include clips showing test routes, common mistakes and videos of manoeuvres."I started making short videos for learner drivers to actually learn something outside of driving lessons and to learn things which they need to know for the driving test," he said."I also do long videos on YouTube so people who can't afford driving lessons have got the opportunity to find out the correct way to do things for the test."So by doing these extra lessons online, it can help bring down those costs."He said while his videos could be a useful tool, they did not mean learners should opt out of formal lessons."I know straight away [if] they have been watching another video," he said."I found that there was a lot of things on there where instructors would say 'this is how you do it, this is how you shouldn't do it' and being very specific to the car they're actually teaching."So what I try to do with mine is make it more universal so it doesn't matter what car you're driving."He warned that people should use online material responsibly. "It needs to be used responsibly and it's looking for those snippets of information to actually improve your driving. You need the practical skills to make those actual decisions."When you then try that road, it's a totally different scenario."Image source, Getty ImagesCarly Brookfield from the DIA said she understood gaining new skills online but said there were risks."I'm a huge advocate of using digital education as something that goes hand in hand with practical training from a professional trainer," she said."That's excellent from the cost perspective, but it's also excellent because the most exposure you can get to driver education in this period, the safer you are."[But] I'm going to be very frank with you here. You could possibly learn enough on YouTube and TikTok and you could possibly fluke a 45-minute driving test," she said."What is the ultimate test of your driving and your driver education to that point is when you [are] on your own and you can cope with those risks."When it comes to road safety, we're talking about life and death."The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA), the UK government body responsible for road safety, said: "Alongside the advice of an Approved Driving Instructor (ADI) and using official learning guides and the Highway Code, there are many ways that learner drivers can supplement their preparation for the driving test."This may include reputable social media content and also private practice with a relative or friend."YouTube and TikTok were approached for comment.Additional reporting by Michela Riva.

schema.headline: Learner drivers use YouTube to cut costs but instructors warn of risks

title: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed
description: The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.The
body: The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.The parliament was launched in 2000 to boost interest in politics among young people and has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18.Once a year, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting.Some MPs and young people say axing it would be a blow for youth democracy, while others say it is not providing value for money.The Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which funds the parliament each year with taxpayer cash, is not committing to giving any more grants to it.A spokesperson for the DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy... giving elected young people a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".It received £453,000 in taxpayer funding in the last year alone with about £2.4m public money spent on it among other youth initiatives between 2017 and 2024.While no final decision has been made on funding beyond March 2027, a government source said: "The government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form."UK Youth Parliament insiders told the BBC that without government funding, it is likely to close.It follows a government review, external published in October last year, which concluded that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people know about it - and some schools felt "excluded from the process".The government says it is working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme that increases their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn.Any new scheme will have a "particular focus on under-represented groups", a government source said.Bobby Forbes, the recently departed chair of the UK Youth Parliament's Youth Select Committee, which works with officials in Westminster, said it gives teenagers "a direct way to scrutinise government and hold decision-makers to account".The 18-year-old said scrapping it "would be a huge mistake and detrimental to youth voice across the UK," and it should be allowed to evolve within its current format.But Jack Rankin, the Conservative MP for Windsor, said last year it "should not receive taxpayers' money and should not sit in the Chamber of the House of Commons".He has said it should be funded by voluntary donations rather than public money. It is understood the funding is spent on the UK Youth Parliament's annual conference, held in Brighton last year, plus travel, communication and support staff.The youth parliament is run by the National Youth Agency, but was previously under the British Youth Council which closed amid financial challenges in 2024.Members are elected every one to two years by voters aged 11 to 18 who live, work or go to school in local authorities. Similar schemes are held for the devolved Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish parliaments.Some politicians started their careers in the UK Youth Parliament, including Labour minister Keir Mather who was became the youngest MP in 2023 - known as the "baby of the House" - when elected aged 25.Peter Swallow, the Labour MP for Bracknell in Berkshire who ran for UK Youth Parliament aged 14, told the BBC the organisation has campaigned successfully on issues such as votes for 16-year-olds.A Bill to lower the voting age from 18 to 16 for all UK elections is currently making its way through Parliament.It would be "short-sighted to cut off funding to a scheme" given these developments, Swallow said."As we face a world where trust in politics is low and young people in particular are doubting the value of democratic institutions, I cannot imagine a more important time for young people to be invited into the heart of our democracy through programmes like UK Youth Parliament."

schema.headline: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed

title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
description: After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my si
body: After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness."Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

schema.headline: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
